card.definition: An adjective is a word that tells about a noun. It tells what kind, how many, or which one.

adverbs-how-when-where.title: Adverbs That Tell How, When, and Where

card.definition: When you list three or more things, put a comma between them. A comma is a small mark that tells the reader to pause.

example.text: I packed a sandwich an apple and a cookie.
example.note: With commas:

then.text: I packed a sandwich, an apple, and a cookie.
then.note: The commas split the list into parts.

card.how: The commas go between the things in the list, so each thing stands on its own.

card.definition: "Your" means it belongs to you. "You're" is a short way to say "you are." The mark in "you're" takes the place of the letter a.

example.text: Is this your lunch box?
example.note: Your tells us the lunch box belongs to you.

more.note: You're means you are.

card.how: If you can swap in "you are," use "you're." If it shows belonging, use "your."

tips.text: Your dog is cute.
You're my best friend.

using-simple-tenses.title: Using Action Verbs in Simple Tenses

card.definition: Verbs change to show when an action happens. "Today" means it happens now. "Yesterday" means it already happened. "Tomorrow" means it will happen later.

example.text: Today Sam walks to school. Yesterday Sam walked to school. Tomorrow Sam will walk to school.
example.note: Walks is now. Walked is past. Will walk is later.

card.how: The word that tells when, like today or yesterday, helps you pick the right verb form.

tips.text: Today Ana sings. Yesterday Ana sang.
Today Leo plays. Tomorrow Leo will play.

items.text: Today, the dog ___ in the yard.

items.right: Yesterday, Ana drew a picture.
items.hint: Yesterday means it already happened, so use the past form.

items.right: Tomorrow, Leo will fly a kite.
items.hint: Tomorrow means it will happen later, so use will plus the verb.

compound-sentences.title: Combining Ideas to Make Compound Sentences
compound-sentences.ask: Choose the sentence that joins the two thoughts the right way.

card.definition: A compound sentence joins two complete thoughts with a word like and, but, or so. Each part could stand alone as a sentence.

example.text: The rain stopped, and the sun came out.

more.note: is one complete thought.
is another. The word and joins them.

card.how: The word and connects two complete thoughts into one longer sentence.

tips.text: Sam likes soccer, but Ana likes tennis.
We can walk, or we can ride our bikes.

items.text: The dog barked. The cat hid.
items.prompt: The dog barked. The cat hid.
options: The dog barked the cat hid.
The dog barked, or the cat hid.
The dog barked, and the cat hid.
The dog barked, the cat hid.
items.right: The dog barked, and the cat hid.
items.hint: Both things happened. Pick the joining word that adds one thought to the other.

items.text: It was cold. We wore our coats.
items.prompt: It was cold. We wore our coats.
options: It was cold, so we wore our coats.
It was cold, we wore our coats.
It was cold we wore our coats.
It was cold, or we wore our coats.

avoiding-run-ons.title: Avoiding Run-Ons
avoiding-run-ons.ask: Fix the run-on. Any right fix counts.

card.definition: A run-on is two complete sentences joined with no punctuation or joining word. Fix it by splitting it into two sentences or by joining it with a comma and a word like and, but, or so.

example.text: The sun came out we went outside.
example.note: This is a run-on. Fix it like this:

then.text: The sun came out, and we went outside.

then.text: Sam was hungry, so he ate a sandwich.

card.definition: A progressive verb shows an action that is happening right now or was happening over time. It uses a form of be plus a verb that ends in ing.

active-or-passive.title: Is the Sentence Active or Passive?
active-or-passive.ask: Is the sentence active or passive?

card.definition: A sentence is active when the subject does the action. A sentence is passive when the subject receives the action, and the verb usually follows a form of be plus a past participle.

example.text: Ana painted the fence.
example.note: Passive:

then.note: In the passive sentence, the fence receives the action.

adverb-describes.title: What Does the Adverb Describe?
adverb-describes.ask: Tap the word the adverb describes.

card.definition: An adverb is a word that describes a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. It often tells how, when, where, or how much.

example.text: The turtle walked slowly across the yard.

adverb-or-adjective.title: Is the Word an Adverb or Adjective?
adverb-or-adjective.ask: Is the word an adjective or an adverb?

card.definition: An adjective describes a noun. An adverb describes a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. To tell them apart, find what the word describes.

card.definition: Adverbs also have comparative and superlative forms. For most short adverbs, add er for two things and est for three or more. For most longer adverbs, use more and most.

card.definition: Articles are the words a, an, and the. They come before a noun and tell whether the noun is general or specific.

example.text: The cat sat on a mat.

sections.title: What a claim is
sections.question: What is the writer trying to prove?
sections.body: A claim is the main opinion in a paragraph. It is a statement the writer must support with facts and reasons.

passage.text: Schools should keep art classes.
Art helps students think in new ways, and it gives every student a chance to shine.

sections.note: The claim is the first sentence. It states the opinion the paragraph will prove.

sections.title: What makes a claim strong
sections.question: Is the claim clear and debatable?
sections.body: A strong claim is clear, specific, and something a reasonable person could disagree with.

passage.text: Recess should last 30 minutes.

sections.note: This claim is clear and specific, and someone could argue for a different length. A weak claim would be “Recess is nice,” which is vague and hard to argue about.

sections.title: Claims in a paragraph
sections.question: Where does the claim belong?
sections.body: The claim usually comes first, as the topic sentence, and the rest of the paragraph supports it.

passage.text: Every student should learn to swim.
Swimming is a life skill, pools are open all year, and lessons are safe with a trained teacher.

sections.note: The claim opens the paragraph, and the sentences after it give reasons.

items.text: Schools should keep art classes. Art helps students think in new ways, and it gives every student a chance to shine.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Art helps students think in new ways, and it gives every student a chance to shine.
items.right: Schools should keep art classes.
items.hint: The claim is the opinion the paragraph will prove.

items.text: The town needs a new library. The old one is too small for the crowds on weekends. A bigger library would hold more books and more computers.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: The town needs a new library.
The old one is too small for the crowds on weekends.
A bigger library would hold more books and more computers.
items.right: The town needs a new library.
items.hint: The claim states what the writer thinks should happen.

items.text: Every family with a yard should consider adopting a dog from the shelter.
items.ask: Which is the stronger claim?
options: Every family with a yard should consider adopting a dog from the shelter.
items.right: Every family with a yard should consider adopting a dog from the shelter.
items.hint: A strong claim is clear, specific, and debatable.

items.text: The school garden should grow food for the cafeteria.
items.ask: Which is the stronger claim?
options: The school garden is the best garden.
The school garden should grow food for the cafeteria.
items.right: The school garden should grow food for the cafeteria.
items.hint: A strong claim is specific and can be supported with reasons.

items.text: Homework should be shorter on Fridays. Students are tired by the end of the week. Shorter homework would still cover the key ideas.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Homework should be shorter on Fridays.
Students are tired by the end of the week.
Shorter homework would still cover the key ideas.
items.right: Homework should be shorter on Fridays.
items.hint: Find the sentence that the other sentences support.

items.text: Evening games end in the dark. Players cannot see the ball after sunset. The soccer field needs new lights.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Evening games end in the dark.
Players cannot see the ball after sunset.
The soccer field needs new lights.
items.right: The soccer field needs new lights.
items.hint: The claim is the opinion the writer wants to prove.

items.text: Every classroom should have a shelf of books students can borrow.
items.ask: Which is the stronger claim?
options: Every classroom should have a shelf of books students can borrow.
items.right: Every classroom should have a shelf of books students can borrow.
items.hint: A strong claim is clear and specific, not vague.

items.text: The park should add a skate ramp. Many students ride skateboards after school. A ramp would give them a safe place to practice.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: The park should add a skate ramp.
Many students ride skateboards after school.
A ramp would give them a safe place to practice.
items.right: The park should add a skate ramp.
items.hint: Ask which sentence gives an opinion and which sentences give reasons.

items.text: Music class should meet twice a week so students can practice their instruments.
items.ask: Which is the stronger claim?
options: Music class should meet twice a week so students can practice their instruments.
items.right: Music class should meet twice a week so students can practice their instruments.
items.hint: A strong claim names something specific that can be argued about.

items.text: Fresh fruit is healthy and easy to eat. The cafeteria should serve fresh fruit every day. Students would choose it over chips.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Fresh fruit is healthy and easy to eat.
The cafeteria should serve fresh fruit every day.
Students would choose it over chips.
items.right: The cafeteria should serve fresh fruit every day.
items.hint: The claim states the opinion the paragraph will prove.

items.text: Libraries are great.
items.ask: Which is the weaker claim?
options: The library should stay open later.
items.right: Libraries are great.
items.hint: A weak claim is vague and hard to support with reasons.

items.text: Bikes should be allowed on the path by the river. The path is wide enough for walkers and riders. Signs would keep everyone safe.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: Bikes should be allowed on the path by the river.
The path is wide enough for walkers and riders.
items.right: Bikes should be allowed on the path by the river.
items.hint: Find the sentence that the rest of the paragraph supports.

claims-evidence-reasoning.title: Identifying Claims, Evidence, and Reasoning
claims-evidence-reasoning.ask: Tap the sentence that does the job.

sections.title: Claims
sections.question: What is the writer trying to prove?
sections.body: A claim is the opinion the writer wants to prove.

passage.text: Our school should start classes later in the morning.
Students learn better when they are rested, and a later start would help everyone focus.

sections.note: The claim is the first sentence. It states the opinion the paragraph will prove.

sections.title: Evidence
sections.question: What fact backs up the claim?
sections.body: Evidence is a fact, an example, or a quote that supports the claim.

passage.text: A study of 200 schools found that students scored higher on morning tests after start times moved later.

sections.note: The evidence is the sentence with the study result. It gives a fact that supports the claim.

sections.title: Reasoning
sections.question: How does the evidence connect to the claim?
sections.body: Reasoning explains why the evidence matters and how it proves the claim.

passage.text: When students sleep longer, they pay attention in class, so later start times lead to better learning.

sections.note: The reasoning is the sentence that links the fact to the claim. It explains why the evidence matters.

items.text: The town library should stay open on Sundays. A survey found that many families can visit the library only on weekends. Opening on Sundays would let those families use the library when they are free.
items.ask: Which sentence is the claim?
options: The town library should stay open on Sundays.
A survey found that many families can visit the library only on weekends.
Opening on Sundays would let those families use the library when they are free.

literary-context.title: Context for Literary Evidence: Speaker, Listener, and Plot Clue

sections.title: What context is
sections.question: What does the reader need to know before the quote?
sections.body: Context is the background a reader needs to understand a piece of evidence from a story. It names who is speaking, who is listening, and what is happening in the plot.

passage.text: In the chapter where the young sailor first meets the captain, the sailor says, 'I have never seen a storm like this.'

sections.note: The context tells us the speaker is the sailor, the listener is the captain, and the plot moment is their first meeting.

sections.title: Why the speaker and listener matter
sections.question: Who says it, and to whom?
sections.body: Knowing the speaker and listener helps the reader judge what the words mean.

passage.text: When the teacher asks the class why the bridge fell, one student answers, 'The wood was rotten.'

sections.note: The speaker is a student, the listener is the teacher, and that tells us the words are an answer to a question.

sections.title: Why the plot clue matters
sections.question: What is happening in the story at this moment?
sections.body: A plot clue places the quote in the story so the reader can follow it.

passage.text: Just after the storm destroys the barn, the farmer looks at the field and says, 'We will rebuild.'

sections.note: The plot clue is the storm destroying the barn, and it explains why the farmer speaks of rebuilding.

nonfiction-context.title: Context for Nonfiction Evidence: Source Information and Reporting Verbs

sections.title: What source information is
sections.question: Where did this fact come from?
sections.body: Source information tells the reader who wrote or said the fact and where it was published, so the reader can judge whether to trust it.

passage.text: Dr. Patel, a scientist who studies oceans, writes in her 2024 book that sea levels are rising.

sections.note: The source information is Dr. Patel, a scientist who studies oceans, and her 2024 book.

sections.title: Reporting verbs
sections.question: Which verb introduces the fact?
sections.body: A reporting verb such as states, explains, notes, or warns introduces a fact from a source. The verb you choose shapes how the reader hears the fact.

passage.text: The report warns that the river is polluted.

sections.note: Warns tells the reader the fact is serious. “The report notes that the river is polluted.” Notes tells the reader the fact is simply stated.

sections.title: Putting them together
sections.question: How do source information and a reporting verb work together?
sections.body: Together they let the reader know who said it and how strongly it was said.

passage.text: In her guide to city parks, ranger Ana Lopez explains that the new trail is safe for families.

sections.note: The source is ranger Ana Lopez and her guide, and explains introduces the fact in a calm, clear way.

sections.title: What a paraphrase is
sections.question: What does it mean to put an idea in your own words?
sections.body: A paraphrase restates someone else's idea using your own words and your own sentence structure. It is not a copy with a few words swapped.

passage.label: Original
passage.text: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds.

passage.label: Good paraphrase
passage.text: When bees move pollen between flowers, plants can produce seeds.

sections.note: The idea is the same, but the words and the sentence shape are new.

sections.title: What plagiarism looks like
sections.question: When is a restatement too close to the original?
sections.body: Copying a sentence and changing one or two words is still plagiarism.

passage.label: Original
passage.text: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps plants make seeds.

passage.label: Too close
passage.text: Bees carry pollen from bloom to bloom, which helps plants make seeds.

sections.note: Only one word changed, so it is still a copy.

sections.title: How to paraphrase safely
sections.question: How do I make it truly my own?
sections.body: Read the idea, look away, write it in your own words, and name the source.

passage.text: The moon has no light of its own.
It shines because it reflects light from the sun.

passage.label: Safe paraphrase
passage.text: Moonlight is really sunlight bouncing off the moon, since the moon does not glow by itself.

sections.note: The words and the shape are new. When you use it in your writing, name the source too.

matching-pronouns-verbs.title: Matching Pronouns and Verbs between Context and Quotations
matching-pronouns-verbs.ask: Choose the sentence that matches the quote.

sections.title: What matching means
sections.question: Why must the words around a quote agree with the quote?
sections.body: When you introduce a quote, the pronouns and verbs in your own sentence must match the pronouns and verbs inside the quote, or the sentence will not make sense.

passage.label: Quote
passage.text: I will finish the poster.

passage.label: Your sentence
passage.text: Maya said that she would finish the poster.

sections.note: She matches I, since both point to Maya, and would finish matches the plan Maya stated. A mismatch would be “Maya said that he would finish the poster,” which changes who does the work.

sections.title: Pronouns
sections.question: Whose words are these?
sections.body: The pronoun in your lead-in must point to the same person as the pronoun in the quote.

passage.label: Quote
passage.text: You played well.

passage.label: Your sentence
passage.text: The coach told the team that they had played well.

sections.note: You in the quote points to the team, so your sentence uses they, not a pronoun for one player.

sections.title: Verbs
sections.question: When did it happen?
sections.body: The verb tense in your lead-in must match the time in the quote.

passage.text: Ana explained that she had read the book.

sections.note: Had read is past, and explained is past, so the times agree. A mismatch would be “Ana explains that she had read the book,” which mixes present and past.

items.right: Maya said that she would finish the poster.
items.hint: The pronoun in your sentence must point to the same person as in the quote.

items.right: The coach told the team that they had played well.

in-text-citations.title: Formatting In-Text Citations
in-text-citations.ask: Choose the citation written the right way.

sections.title: What an in-text citation is
sections.question: How do I show where a fact came from inside my writing?
sections.body: An in-text citation is a short note in parentheses after a fact or quote that names the source.

passage.text: Wolves hunt in packs (Rivera 24).

sections.note: The note in parentheses tells the reader the fact came from Rivera, page 24.

sections.title: Where it goes
sections.question: Where does the citation sit?
sections.body: The citation comes right after the fact or quote, before the period at the end of the sentence.

passage.text: The river is the longest in the state (Lopez 41).

sections.note: The citation sits before the period, not after it.

sections.title: What it contains
sections.question: What goes inside the parentheses?
sections.body: For a book, put the author's last name and the page number, with no comma between them.

passage.text: Bees visit hundreds of flowers in one day (Patel 12).

sections.note: Patel is the author, and 12 is the page.

items.ask: Which sentence formats the citation correctly?
items.right: Wolves hunt in packs (Rivera 24).
items.hint: Check where the period sits compared with the parentheses.

items.ask: Which sentence formats the citation correctly?

The river is the longest in the state (Lopez 41).
items.right: The river is the longest in the state (Lopez 41).
items.hint: Check what sits between the name and the page number.

items.right: Bees visit hundreds of flowers in one day (Patel 12).
items.hint: Look closely at what comes before the page number.

using-transitions.title: Using the Appropriate Transition Words and Phrases

sections.title: What transitions do
sections.question: How do I connect one idea to the next?
sections.body: Transition words and phrases link sentences and show how ideas relate, such as adding, contrasting, or showing cause and effect.

passage.text: The team practiced every day.
As a result, they won the final game.

sections.note: As a result shows that the win followed from the practice.

sections.title: Choosing the right transition
sections.question: Which transition fits the link?
sections.body: For adding an idea, use also, in addition, or furthermore. For contrast, use however, on the other hand, or nevertheless. For cause and effect, use therefore, as a result, or consequently.

passage.text: The rain was heavy.
However, the game went on.

sections.note: However shows a contrast between the rain and the game going on.

sections.title: Where transitions belong
sections.question: Where does the transition sit?
sections.body: A transition usually starts the sentence it connects, followed by a comma.

passage.text: First, the class planned the garden.
Next, they dug the beds.
Finally, they planted the seeds.

sections.note: First, next, and finally show the order of steps.

items.text: The team practiced every day. As a result, they won the final game.
items.right: The team practiced every day. As a result, they won the final game.
items.label: Cause and effect
items.ask: What does as a result show?
items.hint: Ask how winning the final game connects to practicing every day.

items.text: The garden grew tomatoes. ___, it grew peppers.
items.ask: Which transition adds an idea?
items.right: The garden grew tomatoes. In addition, it grew peppers.
items.hint: Ask whether the peppers add to the tomatoes or contrast with them.

items.text: The rain was heavy. ___, the game went on.
items.ask: Which transition shows contrast?
items.right: The rain was heavy. However, the game went on.
items.hint: Ask whether the game going on fits with the heavy rain or goes against it.

items.text: The bus was late. ___, we missed the first class.
items.ask: Which transition shows cause and effect?
items.right: The bus was late. As a result, we missed the first class.
items.hint: Ask whether missing class happened because of the late bus or in contrast to it.

items.text: First, the class planned the garden. Next, they dug the beds. Finally, they planted the seeds.
items.right: First, the class planned the garden. Next, they dug the beds. Finally, they planted the seeds.
items.label: Order of steps
items.ask: What do first, next, and finally show?
items.hint: Ask what first, next, and finally tell you about the steps.

items.text: The movie was long. ___, it was exciting.
items.ask: Which transition fits?
items.right: The movie was long. However, it was exciting.
items.hint: Ask whether exciting goes along with long or goes against it.

items.text: The library is quiet. ___, it has many books.
items.ask: Which transition fits?
items.right: The library is quiet. Furthermore, it has many books.
items.hint: Ask whether having many books adds to being quiet or contrasts with it.

items.text: She studied hard. ___, she passed the test.
items.ask: Which transition fits?
items.right: She studied hard. Therefore, she passed the test.
items.hint: Ask whether passing happened because of studying or in contrast to it.

items.text: At the start of the sentence it connects, followed by a comma
items.ask: Where does a transition usually sit?
items.prompt: "First, the class planned the garden."
options: At the start of the sentence it connects, followed by a comma
At the start of the sentence, with no comma after it
At the end of the sentence, after the period
items.right: At the start of the sentence it connects, followed by a comma
items.hint: Look back at the worked passages and notice where each transition sits and what punctuation follows it.

items.text: We packed our bags. ___, we left for camp.
items.ask: Which transition shows time order?
items.right: We packed our bags. Then, we left for camp.
items.hint: Ask whether leaving came after packing or went against it.

items.text: The soup was hot. ___, it was delicious.
items.ask: Which transition fits?
items.right: The soup was hot. In addition, it was delicious.
items.hint: Ask whether being delicious adds to being hot or goes against it.

items.text: The road was closed. Therefore, we took a different route.
items.right: The road was closed. Therefore, we took a different route.
items.label: Cause and effect
items.ask: What does therefore show?
items.hint: Ask how taking a different route connects to the closed road.

card.definition: Coordinating conjunctions join two equal parts of a sentence, such as two words, two phrases, or two complete sentences. The seven are for, and, nor, but, or, yet, and so. The first letters spell FANBOYS.

example.text: Sam wanted to play soccer, but it was raining.
example.note: But joins two complete sentences.

card.how: Look for for, and, nor, but, or, yet, or so between two equal parts. Each one shows a different link, such as adding, contrasting, or choosing.

tips.text: Maya likes apples and oranges.
We can walk or ride our bikes.

card.definition: Each FANBOYS conjunction has a job. For gives a reason. And adds. Nor gives a negative choice. But shows a contrast. Or gives a choice. Yet shows a surprising contrast. So shows a result.

example.text: She was hungry, so she ate lunch.
example.note: So shows a result.

more.text: She was hungry, but she waited.
more.note: But shows a contrast.

card.how: Read the two parts the conjunction joins, then ask what link it makes. The link tells you the function.

You can swim or sunbathe.

fanboys-punctuate.title: Punctuating FANBOYS
fanboys-punctuate.ask: Put a comma where one is needed, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: When a FANBOYS conjunction joins two complete sentences, put a comma before the conjunction. When it joins two words or phrases, do not use a comma.

example.text: Sam wanted to play, but it rained.
example.note: A comma comes before but because two complete sentences are joined.

more.text: Sam wanted to play soccer and basketball.
more.note: No comma, because and joins two words.

splices-fused.title: Correcting Comma Splices and Fused Sentences

card.definition: A comma splice joins two complete sentences with only a comma. A fused sentence joins two complete sentences with nothing at all. Both are errors. Fix them with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction.

example.text: The bell rang, the students left.

more.text: The bell rang the students left.

card.definition: Conjunctive adverbs connect ideas between sentences or clauses. Common ones are therefore, however, also, moreover, furthermore, meanwhile, otherwise, instead, and nevertheless.

example.text: The bus was late. Therefore, we missed the first class.

card.definition: When a conjunctive adverb starts a sentence, put a comma after it. The conjunctive adverb links the new sentence to the one before it.

conj-adverbs-middle.title: Punctuating Conjunctive Adverbs in the Middle of a Sentence
conj-adverbs-middle.ask: Put the marks where they go.

card.definition: When a conjunctive adverb sits in the middle of a sentence, put a comma before it and a comma after it. The conjunctive adverb breaks the sentence into two parts and links the ideas.

example.text: The bus was late; therefore, we missed the first class.
example.note: The conjunctive adverb therefore is set off by a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

more.text: We missed the first class, therefore, because the bus was late.
more.note: Commas on both sides set the conjunctive adverb apart.

card.how: A conjunctive adverb in the middle of a sentence needs a comma before it and a comma after it. When it joins two complete sentences, a semicolon comes before it instead of a comma.

card.definition: Subordinating conjunctions join a dependent clause to an independent clause. Common ones are since, when, although, because, if, and while. The group is wider, including after, before, unless, until, and though.

example.text: We stayed inside because it rained.
example.note: Because starts the dependent clause because it rained and joins it to the main clause we stayed inside.

card.how: Look for a word that starts a clause that cannot stand alone, and joins it to a clause that can.

long-short-works.title: Recognizing Titles of Long-Form and Short-Form Works
long-short-works.ask: Is the work long-form or short-form?

card.definition: Long-form works are books, movies, plays, albums, magazines, and newspapers. Short-form works are chapters, poems, songs, articles, and short stories. The kind of work tells you how to format its title.

example.text: The Prince and the Pauper
example.note: is a book, a long-form work.

more.note: is a poem, a short-form work.

card.how: Ask how long the work is and how it is published. A work that stands alone is long-form. A work that appears inside a bigger work is short-form.

tips.text: A movie is long-form. A song on an album is short-form. A newspaper is long-form. An article in a newspaper is short-form.

card.definition: Capitalize the first word and all important words in a title. Do not capitalize small words such as a, an, the, and, or, of, and to, unless they are the first word. In print, long-form titles are italicized and short-form titles go in quotation marks.

choosing-fanboys.title: Using the Appropriate FANBOYS
choosing-fanboys.ask: Press the blank to choose the conjunction that fits.

card.definition: Pick the FANBOYS word that fits the link between the two parts. And adds, but contrasts, or chooses, so shows a result, for gives a reason, nor joins negative choices, and yet shows a surprising contrast.

example.text: She studied hard, so she passed.
example.note: So fits because passing is the result of studying.

more.text: She studied hard, but she was nervous.
more.note: But fits because being nervous contrasts with studying hard.

card.how: Read both parts, ask what link they need, then pick the FANBOYS word that makes that link.

correlative-conjunctions.title: Matching Correlative Conjunctions
correlative-conjunctions.ask: Press the blank to choose the word that completes the pair.

card.definition: Correlative conjunctions work in pairs. The pairs are both and, either or, neither nor, not only but also, and whether or.

example.text: Both Ana and Leo finished the race.
example.note: Both pairs with and.

more.text: She not only won the race but also set a record.
more.note: Not only pairs with but also.

card.how: When you see the first half of a pair, the second half must follow. Both needs and. Either needs or. Neither needs nor. Not only needs but also. Whether needs or.

fanboys-errors.title: Correcting FANBOYS Errors
fanboys-errors.ask: Fix the sentence, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: A FANBOYS error happens when the wrong conjunction is used, or when two complete sentences are joined with a FANBOYS word but no comma. Fix it by picking the right word and adding the comma.

example.text: She was hungry but she waited.
example.note: The word but is right, but the comma is missing. Fixed:

then.text: She was hungry, but she waited.

more.text: It rained, so we played outside.
more.note: The word so is wrong, because playing outside is not a result of rain. Fixed:

then.text: It rained, but we played outside.

card.how: First check the link. Does the conjunction match the link? Then check the punctuation. Two complete sentences need a comma before the conjunction.

tips.text: We were tired, but we kept playing.
tips.note: But fits the contrast, and the comma is there.

tips.text: We were hungry, but we ate lunch.
tips.note: But does not fit, because eating lunch does not contrast with being hungry. Fixed:

then.text: We were hungry, so we ate lunch.

items.text: She was hungry but she waited.
items.right: She was hungry, but she waited.
accept: She was hungry, but she waited.
She was hungry, yet she waited.
options: She was hungry, but she waited.
She was hungry, so she waited.
She was hungry but she waited.
items.hint: Check whether each side of but could stand alone, then check the punctuation.

items.text: It rained, so we played outside.
items.right: It rained, but we played outside.
accept: It rained, but we played outside.
It rained, yet we played outside.
options: It rained but we played outside.
It rained, but we played outside.
It rained, so we played outside.
items.hint: Ask whether playing outside is a result of the rain or a contrast with it.

items.text: Maya read a book and Leo read a magazine.
items.right: Maya read a book, and Leo read a magazine.
accept: Maya read a book, and Leo read a magazine.
options: Maya read a book, and Leo read a magazine.

Maya read a book and Leo read a magazine.
items.hint: Check whether each side of and could stand alone, then check the punctuation.

items.text: We were hungry, but we ate lunch.
items.right: We were hungry, so we ate lunch.

options: We were hungry, so we ate lunch.

We were hungry, but we ate lunch.
items.hint: Ask whether eating lunch contrasts with being hungry or follows from it.

The team practiced hard, so they won.
items.hint: Check whether each side of so could stand alone, then check the punctuation.

items.hint: Ask whether true and false can both be the answer or are two choices.

commas-introductory.title: Commas with Introductory Phrases and Clauses
commas-introductory.ask: Put the comma where it goes.

card.definition: An introductory phrase or clause comes at the start of a sentence and sets the scene. Put a comma after it, before the main part of the sentence starts.

example.text: After the rain stopped, we went outside.
example.note: After the rain stopped is an introductory clause, and a comma follows it.

more.text: In the morning, the birds sang.
more.note: In the morning is an introductory phrase, and a comma follows it.

card.how: Find the opening phrase or clause, then add a comma where it ends and the main clause begins.

Under the bridge, a fox made its home.
tips.note: A comma follows under the bridge.

commas-adjectives.title: Commas Separating Adjectives
commas-adjectives.ask: Put a comma where one is needed, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: When two or more adjectives describe the same noun and each one works on its own, put a comma between them. Adjectives like these are called coordinate adjectives.

example.text: The tall, leafy tree shaded the yard.
example.note: Tall and leafy each describe the tree on their own, so a comma goes between them.

more.text: The bright red balloon floated away.
more.note: Bright and red do not each work alone, so no comma goes between them.

card.how: Try swapping the adjectives, and try putting and between them. If both tests work, the adjectives are coordinate and need a comma. If they fail, no comma is needed.

tips.text: A cold, rainy day.
tips.note: Cold and rainy can swap, and you can say cold and rainy, so use a comma.

tips.text: A little black dog.
tips.note: Little and black cannot swap easily, so no comma.

commas-dates.title: Commas with Dates
commas-dates.ask: Put the commas where they go, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: In a date, put a comma between the day and the year, and a comma after the year when the sentence goes on. When only the month and year appear, no comma is needed.

example.note: A comma comes between 2 and 2026.

card.definition: A lot is two words and means a large amount. Alot is not a word at all.

card.definition: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. It tells who does the action or who is described.

example.text: The cat slept on the rug.

sentence-verb.title: Identifying the Verb in a Sentence

card.definition: The verb is the action word or the state of being in a sentence. It tells what the subject does or is.

example.text: The dog barked at the mail carrier.

card.definition: A preposition is a word that shows the link between a noun or pronoun and another word in the sentence. Common prepositions are in, on, under, over, beside, behind, between, through, and with.

dependent-clauses.title: Identifying Dependent Clauses
dependent-clauses.ask: Tap every word of the dependent clause.

card.definition: A dependent clause has a subject and a verb, but it cannot stand alone. It starts with a subordinating word such as because, when, although, if, or while, and it leaves you waiting for more.

example.text: Because it rained, we stayed home.
example.note: Because it rained is the dependent clause. It has a subject and a verb, but it cannot stand alone.

card.how: Find the clause, then ask if it makes sense on its own. If it starts with a subordinating word and leaves you waiting, it is dependent.

conclusion-jobs.title: The Two Jobs of a Conclusion

sections.title: Job one: restate the claim
sections.question: How do I remind the reader what I argued?
sections.body: A conclusion restates the claim in fresh words, so the reader remembers the main point.

passage.label: Claim
passage.text: Schools should keep art classes.

passage.label: Conclusion restatement
passage.text: Art classes belong in every school.

sections.note: The idea is the same, but the words are new.

sections.title: Job two: leave a final thought
sections.question: What should the reader take away?
sections.body: A conclusion ends with a final thought that gives the reader something to remember, such as a call to action or a look ahead.

passage.text: If we protect art classes now, the next generation of artists, builders, and thinkers will thank us.

sections.note: The final thought looks ahead and gives the reader a reason to care.

sections.title: What a conclusion does not do
sections.question: What should I avoid?
sections.body: A conclusion should not bring in new evidence, start a new argument, or repeat the essay word for word.

passage.label: Weak conclusion
passage.text: Art classes are good.
Art classes are good.
Art classes are good.

passage.label: Strong conclusion
passage.text: Art classes help students think in new ways, so every school should keep them.

sections.note: The weak one repeats the same words and adds nothing new, so it fails both jobs.

contractions-possessives.title: Distinguishing Contractions and Possessives
contractions-possessives.ask: Is it a contraction or a possessive?

card.definition: A contraction joins two words with an apostrophe and leaves out letters. A possessive shows ownership and usually uses an apostrophe too, but it does not join two words.

example.text: Don't
example.note: is a contraction of do not.

more.note: is a possessive. The book belongs to Ana.

card.how: Ask what the apostrophe does. If it joins two words and letters are missing, it is a contraction. If it shows ownership, it is a possessive.

tips.note: is a contraction of it is.

tips.note: is a possessive with no apostrophe.

possessive-pronouns.title: Correcting Errors with "Yours," "Hers," "Theirs," and "Ours"
possessive-pronouns.ask: Fix the sentence, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: Yours, hers, theirs, and ours are possessive pronouns. They show ownership, and they never take an apostrophe.

example.text: The red bike is yours.
example.note: Yours shows the bike belongs to you, with no apostrophe.

more.note: Hers shows the book belongs to her, with no apostrophe.

card.how: These words already show ownership on their own. Adding an apostrophe is always wrong.

tips.text: Is this yours?
The house is ours.
The win was theirs.

items.text: The red bike is your's.

sections.title: What a counterargument is
sections.question: What would someone who disagrees say?
sections.body: A counterargument is the strongest point on the other side. Naming it shows the writer has thought about both sides.

passage.label: Claim
passage.text: School should start later.

passage.label: Counterargument
passage.text: Some people say a later start would push sports and jobs into the evening.

sections.note: This names the other side's best point.

sections.title: How to answer it
sections.question: How do I respond without dismissing the other side?
sections.body: A good response takes the counterargument seriously and answers it with a fact or a reason.

passage.text: Sports can end a little later, and studies show that rested students learn more, so the trade is worth it.

sections.note: The response respects the concern and answers it with a fact.

sections.title: Where it belongs
sections.question: Where does the counterargument paragraph go?
sections.body: It usually comes after the main reasons and before the conclusion, so the writer answers the other side and then ends strong.

passage.text: Some people worry about evening sports.
Still, the gain in learning is greater than the change in schedule, so a later start is the better choice.

sections.note: The paragraph answers the concern and leads into the conclusion.

capitalizing-quotes.title: Capitalizing Quotes
capitalizing-quotes.ask: Tap each word whose capital letter is wrong.

card.definition: When a quote starts a sentence, capitalize its first word. When a quote continues a sentence after words such as that, do not capitalize it unless it is a proper noun.

example.text: Ana said, 'The game starts at noon.'
example.note: The game is capitalized because the quote starts the sentence.

more.text: Ana said that the game starts at noon.
more.note: The game is not capitalized because that continues the sentence.

card.how: Ask where the quote sits. A quote that starts a sentence gets a capital first word. A quote that follows that stays lower case.

card.definition: A dialogue quote is a character's exact words in a story. A flow quote is a short quote woven into your own sentence so the sentence reads smoothly. Both need quotation marks and the right punctuation.

example.text: 'Where are you going?' asked Ana.

then.text: Ana said the fair was 'the best part of summer.'
then.note: The quote fits inside the writer's sentence.

card.how: For dialogue, put the quote in quotation marks, add a comma or question mark inside the closing mark, and name the speaker. For a flow quote, weave the quoted words into your sentence so it reads as one smooth sentence.

dialogue-colon-quotes.ask: Put a comma or a colon before the quote.

card.definition: A colon quote is a quote introduced with a colon after a complete sentence. The colon sets up the quote like a drumroll. A dialogue quote uses a comma or question mark instead.

formal-informal.title: Recognizing Language That Is Too Formal or Too Informal
formal-informal.ask: Choose the language that fits the setting.

card.definition: Formal language is polite and careful, and it fits school essays, letters to adults, and reports. Informal language is casual and fits friends, texts, and notes. Language is too formal or too informal when it does not fit the setting.

example.note: is too informal for a letter to the principal.

verb-tenses.title: Identifying Verbs in Simple, Progressive, and Perfect Tenses

card.definition: Verbs change form to show time. Simple tenses show one time: past, present, or future. Progressive tenses show an action in progress, using a form of be plus ing. Perfect tenses show an action finished before another time, using a form of have plus a past participle.

example.text: She walked.
example.note: Simple past.

more.note: Present progressive, an action in progress.
Present perfect, an action finished before now.

card.how: Look at the verb form. The main verb alone, or will plus the verb, means simple. A form of be plus ing means progressive. A form of have plus a past participle means perfect.

tips.text: They played.
They are playing.
They have played.

card.definition: A pronoun takes the place of a noun. It lets you talk about a person, place, or thing without repeating its name.

fragments-in-dialogue.title: Recognizing Fragments in Dialogue
fragments-in-dialogue.ask: Tap every word of the fragment.

card.definition: A fragment is a group of words that looks like a sentence but is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought. In dialogue, short replies like "Yes" or "Not yet" are fine in real speech, but a fragment is still not a sentence.

example.text: 'Where did you go?' 'To the store.'
example.note: To the store is a fragment. It has no subject and no verb.

card.how: Check every line of dialogue for a subject and a verb. If one is missing, the line is a fragment.

tips.text: 'Are you coming?' 'In a minute.'
tips.note: In a minute is a fragment.

pronoun-subject-sentences.title: Recognizing Sentences with Pronoun Subjects
pronoun-subject-sentences.ask: Tap the pronoun that is the subject.

card.definition: A sentence can have a pronoun as its subject. The pronoun takes the place of a noun, but the sentence is still complete as long as it has a verb and a finished thought.

example.text: They built a fort in the yard.
example.note: They is a pronoun, and it is the subject. Built is the verb. The sentence is complete.

card.how: Find the verb first, then ask who or what did it. If the answer is a pronoun like they, she, it, or we, the sentence has a pronoun subject and is complete.

that-which-especially.title: Sentences and Fragments with "That," "Which," and "Especially"
that-which-especially.ask: Is it a sentence or a fragment?

card.definition: Words like that, which, and especially often start a group of words that adds detail, and that group alone is a fragment. A clause starting with that or which needs a main clause to finish the thought.

example.text: The book that I borrowed was about space.
example.note: That I borrowed is a clause that adds detail, and the whole sentence is complete.

more.note: Alone, it is a fragment. Fix it:

then.text: The book that I borrowed is due on Monday.

card.how: Find the clause that starts with that or which. Ask whether it can stand alone. If it cannot, it is a fragment unless it is joined to a main clause.

tips.text: The kite, which was red, flew high.
Which was red.
tips.note: Alone, it is a fragment. Fix it:

then.text: The ball, which was red, rolled away.

thesis-fact-opinion.title: Is the Thesis a Fact or Opinion?
thesis-fact-opinion.ask: Tap the sentence that does the job.

sections.title: Facts
sections.question: Can the statement be proven true or false?

passage.text: The school library holds 4,000 books.

sections.note: This is a fact. It can be checked by counting the books.

sections.title: Opinions
sections.question: Does the statement say what someone thinks or feels?

passage.text: The school library is the best room in the building.

sections.note: This is an opinion. It says what the writer thinks, and another person could disagree.

sections.title: Debatable theses
sections.question: Can a reasonable person disagree with it?

passage.text: The school library should stay open later so students have more time to read.

sections.note: This is a debatable thesis. It is an opinion that a reader can argue for or against.

items.text: The river is 200 miles long. The river is the most beautiful place in the state. The state should protect the river from pollution.
items.ask: Which sentence is the thesis?
options: The river is the most beautiful place in the state.
The state should protect the river from pollution.
items.right: The state should protect the river from pollution.
items.hint: A thesis is a debatable opinion, not a fact.

hook-agreeing.title: Selecting a Strong Hook 1: Agreeing
hook-agreeing.ask: Tap the sentence that does the job.

sections.title: What is a hook?
sections.question: Does the first sentence grab the reader?

passage.text: Most students agree that homework takes too long.

sections.note: This hooks the reader by starting with something many people already believe.

sections.title: Why start with agreement?
sections.question: Does it make the reader nod before you argue?

passage.text: Everyone knows that practice makes a player better.
But practice only helps when the drills match the game.

sections.note: The first sentence gets the reader to agree, so the second sentence lands harder.

sections.title: What makes a hook weak?
sections.question: Does it just restate the topic?

passage.label: Weak hook
passage.text: This essay is about homework.

passage.label: Strong hook
passage.text: Most students spend an hour a night on homework, but does it help them learn?

sections.note: The weak hook tells the reader the topic but gives no reason to keep reading. The strong hook asks a question the reader wants answered.

items.text: Most students agree that homework takes too long. They finish one subject and start another, and the evening disappears.
items.ask: Which sentence is the hook?
options: Most students agree that homework takes too long.
They finish one subject and start another, and the evening disappears.
items.right: Most students agree that homework takes too long.
items.hint: Look for the sentence that grabs the reader and makes them want to read on.

items.text: Everyone knows that practice makes a player better. But practice only helps when the drills match the game.
items.ask: Which sentence starts with agreement?
options: Everyone knows that practice makes a player better.
But practice only helps when the drills match the game.
items.right: Everyone knows that practice makes a player better.
items.hint: Starting with something many people believe gets the reader to nod.

items.text: This essay is about homework. Homework is given every night.
items.ask: Which sentence is a weak hook?
items.right: This essay is about homework.
items.hint: A weak hook only restates the topic and gives no reason to keep reading.

items.text: Most families agree that dinner together matters. The table is where stories get told.
items.ask: Which sentence is the hook?
options: Most families agree that dinner together matters.
The table is where stories get told.
items.right: Most families agree that dinner together matters.
items.hint: Look for the sentence that grabs the reader and makes them want to read on.

items.text: Everybody likes a good story. A good story pulls you in from the first line.
items.ask: Which sentence starts with agreement?
options: A good story pulls you in from the first line.
items.right: Everybody likes a good story.
items.hint: Starting with something many people believe gets the reader to nod.

items.text: This paper is about the library. The library has many books.

options: This paper is about the library.

redundant-wordy.title: Recognizing Redundant, Unnecessary, and Wordy Phrases
redundant-wordy.ask: Tap the sentence that does the job.

sections.title: Redundant phrases
sections.question: Does one word already say what the other word says?

passage.label: Fixed

sections.title: Unnecessary words

sections.title: Wordy phrases
sections.question: Can a short phrase say the same thing?

vague-words.title: Identifying Vague Words and Phrases 1
vague-words.ask: Tap the sentence that does the job.

sections.title: What vague words are
sections.question: Does the word give the reader a clear picture?

passage.label: Vague
passage.text: The trip was nice.

passage.label: Clear
passage.text: The trip was sunny, and we swam every day.

sections.note: The word “nice” is vague. It does not say what was good about the trip.

sections.title: How to spot them
sections.question: Could the word mean many different things?

passage.label: Vague
passage.text: She did a lot of stuff at camp.

passage.label: Clear
passage.text: She swam, hiked, and cooked at camp.

sections.note: The phrase “a lot of stuff” is vague. It could mean swimming, hiking, cooking, or anything else.

sections.title: How to replace them
sections.question: What exact word says what you mean?

passage.text: The trip was exciting because we climbed a tall hill and cooked dinner over a fire.

sections.note: The exact words replace the vague word “nice” with clear details.

citation-end-marks.title: Question Marks and Exclamation Points with Citations

card.definition: When a quoted sentence ends with a question mark or an exclamation point, that mark stays inside the closing quotation mark. The citation still goes after the quote, and the sentence ends with a period after the citation.

identifying-modifiers.title: Identifying Modifiers
identifying-modifiers.ask: Tap every word of the modifier.

card.definition: A modifier is a word or phrase that describes another word in the sentence. It usually tells what kind, how, when, or where.

example.note: With the red collar is the modifier. It describes the dog.

restrictive-clauses.title: Punctuating Restrictive and Nonrestrictive Clauses
restrictive-clauses.ask: Put commas around the clause if it only adds detail, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: A restrictive clause is needed to know which person or thing you mean, so it takes no commas. A nonrestrictive clause adds extra detail that is not needed, so it is set off with commas.

example.text: The student who won the race smiled.
example.note: Who won the race is restrictive, so no commas.

more.text: Ana, who won the race, smiled.
more.note: Who won the race is extra detail about Ana, so it takes commas.

card.how: Ask whether the clause is needed to tell which one. If yes, leave out the commas. If no, set it off with commas.

tips.note: That I borrowed is needed, so no commas.

tips.note: Which was old is extra detail, so it takes commas.

shared-unshared.title: Is the Possession Shared or Unshared?
shared-unshared.ask: Is the possession shared or unshared?

card.definition: Shared possession means two or more people own one thing together. Only the last name takes an apostrophe and -s. Unshared possession means each person owns a separate thing, so every name takes an apostrophe and -s.

example.note: They share one garden, so only Leo's takes the apostrophe.

more.note: They each have their own garden, so both names take the apostrophe.

card.how: Ask whether the owners share one thing or each own one. One shared thing means one apostrophe, on the last name. Separate things mean an apostrophe on every name.

card.definition: A subject pronoun does the action of the verb. An object pronoun receives the action or follows a preposition. Subject pronouns are I, you, he, she, it, we, and they. Object pronouns are me, you, him, her, it, us, and them.

example.text: She gave the book to him.
example.note: She is a subject pronoun because she does the giving. Him is an object pronoun because he receives the book.

gerund-pronouns.title: Using Possessive Pronouns with Gerunds
gerund-pronouns.ask: Choose the pronoun that fits before the -ing word.

card.definition: A gerund is a verb form ending in -ing that works as a noun. When a pronoun comes before a gerund, use the possessive form, like his, her, my, or their, not the object form.

example.text: His singing won the contest.
example.note: Singing is a gerund. His is the possessive pronoun before it.

card.how: Find the -ing word that works as a noun. The pronoun right before it should be possessive, because the -ing word is a thing, and the pronoun shows whose thing it is.

tips.note: Her is possessive before the gerund dancing.

reflexive-pronouns.title: Using Reflexive Pronouns
reflexive-pronouns.ask: Choose the pronoun that points back to the subject.

card.definition: A reflexive pronoun ends in -self or -selves and points back to the subject. Use it when the subject and the object are the same person or thing. The forms are myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, and themselves.

example.text: Ana taught herself to juggle.
example.note: Herself points back to Ana. Ana is both the teacher and the learner.

card.how: Ask whether the object is the same person as the subject. If yes, use the reflexive form. If no, use a regular object pronoun.

indefinite-agreement.title: Pronoun Agreement with Indefinite Antecedents

card.definition: A professional title is capitalized when it comes before a person's name or when it is used as part of a direct address. It stays lowercase when it simply describes the person's job after the name.

example.text: captain ruiz led the rescue team.
example.note: The title captain comes before the name Ruiz, so the sentence becomes

then.text: Captain Ruiz led the rescue team.

card.how: A title used as part of a name is a proper noun, so it takes a capital letter.

tips.text: Judge Alvarez will hear the case.
tips.note: Judge is capitalized before a name.

tips.text: Rosa Alvarez, a judge in our town, will hear the case.
tips.note: Judge stays lowercase because it describes her job.

items.text: captain ruiz led the rescue team.
items.right: Captain Ruiz led the rescue team.
items.hint: A professional title is capitalized when it comes before a name.

items.right: Rosa Alvarez, a judge in our town, will hear the case.

cap-space.title: Capitalizing Things in Space
cap-space.ask: Tap each word whose capital letter is wrong, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: The names of planets, stars, galaxies, and other specific things in space are capitalized. Earth is capitalized when it names our planet. The everyday words sun and moon stay lowercase.

card.how: Specific things in space are proper nouns, so they take capital letters.

cap-subjects.title: Capitalizing Academic Subjects
cap-subjects.ask: Tap each word whose capital letter is wrong, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: The names of specific school subjects that come from a language, a place, or a person's name are capitalized, like Spanish, French, and English. General subjects like math, science, and history stay lowercase, unless they are part of a course title.

example.text: i take spanish and math this year.
example.note: The word I and the language spanish need capitals, but math stays lowercase, so the sentence becomes

then.text: I take Spanish and math this year.

card.how: Language names are proper nouns, so they take capital letters. General subject names are common nouns.

card.definition: The verb in a sentence must agree with its subject in number. A singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb.

agree-compound.ask: Choose the verb that agrees with the subject.

card.definition: A compound subject joins two or more subjects with and. When the parts are joined by and, the subject is plural, so the verb is plural. When the parts name the same single person or thing, the subject stays singular.

example.text: Sam and Ana walk to school together.

then.text: walk
then.note: is plural.

tips.note: Two animals, so the verb is plural.

verb-or-verbal.title: Is It a Verb or Not a Verb?

card.definition: A verb is a word that shows an action or a state of being, and it can be the main verb of a sentence. A verbal looks like a verb but acts as a different part of speech: an infinitive acts as a noun, adjective, or adverb, a participle acts as an adjective, and a gerund acts as a noun. A verbal can never be the main verb of a sentence.

example.text: Swimming is good exercise.
example.note: The word

then.text: swimming
then.note: looks like a verb, but it is the subject of the sentence, so it is a gerund, not a verb.

card.how: Ask what job the word does. If it is the main verb, it is a verb. If it acts as a noun or adjective, it is a verbal.

tips.note: To read is an infinitive, not a verb.

verbal-functions.title: Identifying the Function of Verbals
verbal-functions.ask: What does the verbal in bold do?

card.definition: Every verbal has a job in a sentence. A gerund acts as a noun, so it can be a subject or an object. A participle acts as an adjective, so it describes a noun. An infinitive can act as a noun, an adjective, or an adverb.

example.text: To win takes practice.
example.note: The infinitive

then.text: to win
then.note: is the subject of the sentence, so it acts as a noun.

card.how: Ask what the verbal does. If it names something, it acts as a noun. If it describes a noun, it acts as an adjective. If it tells why or how, it acts as an adverb.

tips.note: Swimming is a gerund acting as a subject.

tips.note: Barking is a participle acting as an adjective.

card.definition: Cite is a verb that means to quote or refer to a source as evidence, sight is a noun or verb that refers to vision or something seen, and site is a noun that means a location or place where something happens or is built.

example.text: Ana had to cite her source in the essay, and she visited the site of the old mill where she caught sight of a heron.
example.note: Cite: verb meaning to quote a source. Site: noun meaning a location. Sight: noun meaning something seen.

card.how: Each word sounds alike but has a different spelling and meaning, so the meaning of the sentence tells you which spelling fits.

card.definition: Scene is a noun that means a place, a view, or a part of a play, film, or story, while seen is the past participle of see and means viewed or noticed in the past.

card.definition: Farther refers to a greater physical distance, while further refers to a greater extent, degree, or amount, or to something additional in a discussion or idea.

anyway-anyways.title: "Anyway" vs. "Anyways"
anyway-anyways.ask: Choose the word that fits formal writing.

card.definition: Anyway is the standard adverb that means in any case, regardless, or in any way, while anyways is a nonstandard informal variant that should be avoided in school and formal writing.

example.text: The rain continued, but Leo decided to practice anyway.
example.note: Anyway: standard adverb meaning in any case.

card.how: In essays, reports, and other formal writing, use anyway, and save anyways only for casual speech if you use it at all.

card.definition: Altogether is an adverb that means completely or in total, while all together is a phrase that means all in one place or all at the same time.

card.definition: Prejudice is a noun that means an unfair opinion formed before knowing the facts, while prejudiced is an adjective that describes a person or view shaped by such an unfair opinion.

example.text: Prejudice can harm a community, and a prejudiced remark can hurt a classmate.

card.how: If the word names the unfair opinion itself, use prejudice, and if it describes a person, statement, or attitude, use prejudiced.

colons-semicolons.title: Connecting Clauses with Colons and Semicolons
colons-semicolons.ask: Put a colon or a semicolon between the two parts.

card.definition: A colon introduces an explanation, a list, or a second clause that develops the first, and a semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction.

example.text: Leo had one goal: to finish the race. The crowd was loud; the runners stayed focused.
example.note: Colon: introduces the goal. Semicolon: joins two related independent clauses.

conj-adverbs-clauses.title: Connecting Clauses with Conjunctive Adverbs 1
conj-adverbs-clauses.ask: Put the marks around the conjunctive adverb.

card.definition: A conjunctive adverb, such as however, therefore, or meanwhile, connects two independent clauses, and it needs a semicolon before it and a comma after it when it joins them in one sentence.

example.text: Ana studied all week; therefore, she felt ready for the test.
example.note: Semicolon: before the conjunctive adverb. Therefore: conjunctive adverb meaning as a result. Comma: after the conjunctive adverb.

card.how: The semicolon separates the two complete sentences, the conjunctive adverb shows the logical link between them, and the comma marks the end of the conjunctive adverb.

hyphen-fractions.title: Hyphens with Fractions
hyphen-fractions.ask: Choose the fraction written the right way.

card.definition: A fraction used as a noun or an adjective takes a hyphen between its two parts, such as one-half, two-thirds, or three-quarters, when it is spelled out in words.

example.text: Ana ate one-half of the sandwich, and two-thirds of the class finished early.
example.note: One-half: hyphenated fraction. Two-thirds: hyphenated fraction.

card.how: The hyphen joins the two number words into one fraction, whether the fraction names an amount or describes a noun.

hyphen-affixes.title: Hyphens with Prefixes and Suffixes 1
hyphen-affixes.ask: Choose the word joined the right way.

card.definition: Most prefixes and suffixes join a word without a hyphen, such as rewrite or hopeful, but a hyphen is needed when the prefix ends with the same vowel the root starts with, when the word would be hard to read, or when the root is a capital letter or a number.

example.text: Leo will rewrite the draft, but he will re-enter the lab after lunch.
example.note: Rewrite: prefix joined without a hyphen. Re-enter: hyphen after re because the root starts with e.

hyphen-clarity.title: Hyphens for Clarity
hyphen-clarity.ask: Choose the words that say what the sentence means.

card.definition: A hyphen is used for clarity when it prevents a misreading, separates a confusing pair of letters, or shows that words belong together as one idea rather than two separate ideas.

example.text: Leo will re-cover the chair, not recover the chair after his illness.
example.note: Re-cover: hyphen shows cover again. Recover: no hyphen means get well.

card.how: If the sentence could be read the wrong way without the hyphen, add it, because the hyphen guides the reader to the intended meaning.

list-cue-words.title: Introducing Lists with Cue Words
list-cue-words.ask: Put the marks the list needs, or say it is right as it is.

card.definition: A list can be introduced by cue words such as for example, such as, or including, and those cue words need the punctuation that fits the sentence, usually a comma before for example and no colon after such as or including.

example.text: Ana likes outdoor sports, for example, hiking and kayaking, and she likes games such as chess and cards.
example.note: For example: cue phrase set off with commas. Such as: cue phrase that needs no colon.

card.how: For example is an interrupting phrase that takes commas around it, while such as and including flow directly into the list with no colon and no comma before the list.

card.definition: Parallel structure means that items joined in a list, a pair, or a comparison use the same grammatical form, such as all nouns, all verbs ending in ing, or all clauses starting the same way.

parallel-match.title: Matching Parallel Elements 1
parallel-match.ask: Choose the words that match the other items.

card.definition: To match parallel elements, revise the item that breaks the pattern so it uses the same form as the other items, such as changing a noun to a gerund or an infinitive to match the rest of the list.

example.text: Ana likes reading, writing, and to speak
example.note: becomes

then.text: Ana likes reading, writing, and speaking.
then.note: To speak: nonparallel infinitive. Speaking: revised gerund to match reading and writing.
